theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Explain how you would choose the right graduated device for each of these electrical jobs: measuring a 40 m cable route, setting out box heights, checking a conductor's size, and measuring a cable's overall diameter.
essays.modelAnswer: I choose a device whose resolution is finer than the accuracy the job needs, but no finer than is practical. For a 40 m cable route I would use a laser distance meter, or a 30 m fibreglass tape or a measuring wheel outdoors, because the length only needs to be right to a few centimetres. For box heights I would use a steel tape from finished floor level, with a laser level to keep the boxes in line, as millimetres matter. To check a conductor's size I would use an outside micrometer, because a small change in diameter changes the area a lot, so I need readings to 0.01 mm. For a cable's overall diameter I would use a vernier or digital caliper, closed lightly so the sheath is not squashed. Near live parts I would only use non-conductive devices.
markingPoints: Matches resolution to the accuracy the job needs
Long route: laser meter, fibreglass tape or wheel
Box heights: tape from FFL, with a level line
Conductor size: micrometer, with reason
Cable diameter: caliper used lightly (and non-conductive devices near live parts)

essays.stem: Describe how to find the size (cross-sectional area) of an unmarked solid conductor and of an unmarked stranded conductor by measuring. Give a worked example of each.
essays.modelAnswer: First I make sure the cable is not connected to any supply. For a solid conductor, I strip a short length of insulation without nicking the copper, zero-check a micrometer, and measure the diameter in two directions, using the ratchet. I work out the area with π × d² ÷ 4. For example, 1.78 mm gives 3.14 × 1.78 × 1.78 ÷ 4 = about 2.5 mm². For a stranded conductor I count the strands and measure the diameter of one strand, because measuring across the bundle includes the gaps. If there are 7 strands of 0.85 mm, one strand is 3.14 × 0.85 × 0.85 ÷ 4 = about 0.57 mm², and 7 strands make about 4 mm². I compare the answer with the nearest standard size and record it with the device used.
markingPoints: Checks the cable is disconnected and strips without nicking
Uses a zero-checked micrometer with the ratchet, two directions
Correct formula and worked solid example
Stranded: measures one strand and multiplies by the number of strands
Compares with the nearest standard size and records it

essays.stem: Explain the safety precautions you would take when measuring in and around electrical installations, including inside boards, at height and with laser devices.
essays.modelAnswer: Wherever possible I measure with the circuits isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after. I remember that the incoming side of a board stays live even with the main switch off, so I keep away from it. Near any part that could be live I use a non-conductive fibreglass tape or rule, never a steel tape, which conducts and can spring back into live parts. At height I use a sound step-ladder or tower and do not over-reach to stretch a tape. With a laser distance meter or laser level I never look into the beam or point it at anyone's eyes, and I warn others when it is in use. I keep tapes out of walkways so no one trips, and I follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead with a tester checked before and after
Incoming side stays live: keep clear
Non-conductive tapes and rules near live parts; why steel is dangerous
Safe access at height, no over-reaching
Laser eye safety (and keeping tapes out of walkways)

essays.stem: Describe how you would set out the positions of light points, switches and outlet boxes in a room from a drawing, so that they are level, in line and at the right heights.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the drawing for its scale and the written dimensions, and note the heights, which are given above finished floor level. I find out how thick the floor finish will be, so I can allow for it. I choose a datum, such as one corner or a centre line, and measure all positions from it so errors do not add up. For the ceiling lights, I find the room's centre lines and work out the spacing, for example half a space at each end. For switches and outlets, I set a laser level or mark a level line round the room at the right height and measure positions along it with a tape. I mark each position clearly, then check the marks against the drawing and with a second person before any fixing or drilling is done.
markingPoints: Uses written dimensions and heights above FFL
Allows for the floor finish
Measures from one datum
Works out even spacing for lights
Uses a level line, then checks all marks before fixing

essays.stem: Explain how you would check the Centre's tapes, rules, calipers, micrometers and laser meters for accuracy, and how you would keep the records.
essays.modelAnswer: I would give each device a number and list it in a register with its type, range and the date its next check is due. Tapes and rules would be compared with a reference tape that is kept only for checking, at a few points along their length. Calipers and micrometers would be zero-checked, then checked with gauge blocks or setting standards at several sizes across their range. Laser meters would be compared with the reference tape over a known distance, such as 5 m and 10 m. For each check I record the date, the readings, the error found and who did it. Any device outside the limits set by the assessor or the maker is tagged and removed from use, and work done with it since the last good check is reviewed. Devices are also checked after any drop or knock.
markingPoints: Numbered register with due dates
Tapes and laser meters checked against a reference over known lengths
Calipers and micrometers checked with gauge blocks or standards
Records: date, readings, error, name
Faulty devices tagged out and recent work reviewed

essays.stem: A trainee's box heights on a job are all 15 to 20 mm out. As team leader, explain how you would find the cause and put it right.
essays.modelAnswer: I would stop the fixing of any more boxes and re-measure a few myself, so I know the size of the error. Then I would watch the trainee measure. Possible causes include measuring from bare concrete instead of allowing for the floor finish, using a tape with a damaged or bent hook, reading the tape at an angle, or measuring each box from the last one so the errors add up. I would check the tape against a good one. Once I find the cause, I would explain it to the trainee and show the right method, such as working from a level line set from one datum. The boxes that are out of tolerance would be reset before the walls are finished. I would record what happened and check the trainee's next work.
markingPoints: Stops the work and re-measures to confirm the error
Watches the method and checks the tape
Names likely causes (datum, floor finish, hook, parallax, added errors)
Coaches the right method
Corrects the boxes, records and follows up

essays.stem: Explain how to use a scale rule to take cable lengths off an electrical layout drawing, and describe the limits of doing this.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the scale written in the title block, such as 1:50 or 1:100, and pick the matching edge of the scale rule. I lay the rule along each straight part of the cable route and read the real length straight off the scale, or measure in millimetres and multiply by the scale. I add up the straight parts, then add the drops down walls to switches and outlets, and allowances for terminations and waste. The limits are that paper can stretch or shrink, copies may not be printed at the right size, and the drawing does not show the height changes or the real route round beams. If the drawing says 'Do not scale', I use the written dimensions. So I treat scaled lengths as an estimate and check on site before ordering a large amount.
markingPoints: Checks the drawing's scale and uses the matching scale
Measures each part of the route and adds them
Adds drops, terminations and waste
Limits: copies, paper changes, hidden heights and routes
Uses written sizes where given and checks on site

essays.stem: Compare a steel tape, a fibreglass tape, a laser distance meter and a measuring wheel. Give one good use and one limitation of each.
essays.modelAnswer: A steel tape is stiff and accurate, so it is good for setting out box heights and short runs. Its limitation is that it conducts electricity, so it must not be used near live parts. A fibreglass tape does not conduct and comes in long lengths, so it is good for long runs and near electrical equipment. It can stretch a little over time and sags over long spans. A laser distance meter lets one person measure long distances quickly, such as across a hall or up to a ceiling. It needs a clear target, can be fooled by glass or shiny surfaces, and needs care with the beam and the battery. A measuring wheel is quick for long distances along the ground, such as a trench route. It is not accurate on rough or soft ground or for short lengths.
markingPoints: Steel tape: use and the conducting hazard
Fibreglass tape: use near electrical equipment; stretch or sag
Laser meter: one-person long distances; target and eye-safety limits
Measuring wheel: ground routes; poor on rough ground or short lengths
Sensible choice for the job overall

essays.stem: Explain how graduated measuring devices should be cared for in Jamaica's hot, humid and salty air, both in the workshop and in the work van.
essays.modelAnswer: After use I wipe each device clean and dry, because sweat, dust and salt air cause rust and wear. Steel parts of rules, calipers and micrometers get a light film of oil before storing. Each device goes back in its own case so it is not knocked. A micrometer is stored with its faces slightly apart. Tapes are wound back slowly so the hook is not damaged, and wet tapes are dried before winding them in. In the van, devices are kept in a closed box out of the sun, because heat can affect accuracy and damage batteries and displays, and they are not left loose to rattle about. Laser meters have their lens kept clean and the batteries removed if stored for a long time. Any damage is reported and the device tagged.
markingPoints: Clean and dry after use; reason (salt, sweat, rust)
Light oil on steel parts; own case
Micrometer faces apart; tapes wound in carefully and dried
In the van: closed box, out of the sun, secured
Laser and electronic care; report and tag damage

essays.stem: Describe how to use and read an outside micrometer to check conductor sizes, and how to record the results so that they are useful.
essays.modelAnswer: I choose a 0–25 mm micrometer and wipe the anvil and spindle faces clean. I close them gently using the ratchet and check that it reads zero; if not, I adjust it or note the error. I hold the micrometer by its frame, put the bare conductor square between the faces and turn the ratchet until it clicks two or three times. I read the sleeve for whole and half millimetres, then add the thimble reading in hundredths. For example, 1.5 mm on the sleeve and 28 on the thimble gives 1.78 mm. I measure in two directions to check for flattening. I record the reading in millimetres, the area worked out, the size it matches, the circuit or cable, the micrometer's number, the date and my name, so the result can be checked later.
markingPoints: Cleans faces and checks the zero with the ratchet
Holds by the frame and uses the ratchet on the conductor
Reads sleeve and thimble correctly, with an example
Measures in two directions
Records reading, unit, size, device number, date and name

practical1.title: Set out and check a lighting and outlet layout on a training wall
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a layout drawing for a small room (for example three ceiling light points, two switches and four outlets) with heights given above finished floor level and a floor finish thickness to allow for. As a group, choose a datum, set out every position on the training wall and ceiling board in chalk or pencil, using tapes, a level or laser level and a folding rule. Each member sets out at least two positions. Then the group checks all the positions against the drawing and the tolerance the assessor gives, records every measurement on a set-out sheet with units and the device used, and corrects anything out of tolerance. Work only on dead training walls; nothing is drilled. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Layout drawing and tolerance from the assessor
Steel tapes and a fibreglass tape
Laser distance meter (if the Centre has one)
Chalk line, pencils and masking tape
photos: The group checking the drawing and choosing the datum
The level line marked round the training wall
Light positions marked on the ceiling board with their spacing
Switch and outlet positions marked, with a tape showing the height
checklist: Read the drawing correctly and allowed for the floor finish
Measured all positions from the agreed datum
Used each device correctly (tape hook, level, laser safety)
Set out positions within the given tolerance
Recorded each measurement with its unit and the device used
Checked another member's work and corrected errors
Returned devices clean to their cases
safety: Never point a laser at anyone's eyes
Use a step-ladder only when it is sound, footed and on level ground
Keep tapes and leads out of walkways
Work only on the dead training walls the assessor names

practical2.title: Identify conductor and cable sizes by measurement, and run a device check
practical2.brief: Part A: the assessor gives the group a set of unmarked, disconnected conductor and cable samples (solid and stranded). Each member measures at least two samples with a zero-checked micrometer or caliper, works out the cross-sectional area, names the nearest standard size, and measures the overall cable diameter to work out a minimum bend radius from the factor the assessor gives. Part B: the group checks the Centre's tapes, calipers and micrometers against a reference tape and gauge blocks or setting standards, records the errors, and tags any device that is outside the assessor's limits. The group writes up both parts on record sheets and updates the device register. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Unmarked conductor and cable samples (solid and stranded), disconnected
0–25 mm outside micrometers and vernier or digital calipers
Reference tape and gauge blocks or setting standards
Tapes and rules to be checked
Record sheets, device register and faulty tags
photos: A member measuring a single strand of a stranded conductor
The worked area calculations on the record sheet
A cable's overall diameter being measured with a caliper
A tape being compared with the reference tape
The updated device register, with any faulty device tagged
checklist: Measured conductors correctly, using the ratchet and two directions
Worked out area and named the right standard size
Worked out the minimum bend radius correctly
Checked devices against the reference and recorded the errors
Tagged and reported any faulty device
Cleaned and stored all devices correctly
safety: Use only disconnected samples; never measure a conductor that is connected to a supply
Strip insulation with the blade away from the body and hands
Wear safety glasses when cutting conductors
Put copper offcuts in the scrap bin
